title: Who Gets Paid When AI Does the Shopping? | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: a16z Growth partners argue AI shopping assistants threaten marketplace profits not by replicating fulfillment but by capturing discovery, putting ad-heavy profit pools (Amazon's $69B ads vs $34B ex-AWS operating income) at risk. Platforms with ad businesses to protect (Amazon) block agents like Muse, while software/payments rails (Shopify, Toast, Square) and share-seekers (Instacart) lean in; outcomes hinge on incremental demand versus rerouted orders and on bargaining leverage.

insights.claim: AI shopping assistants do not need to replicate Amazon's warehouse network to pressure Amazon's profits; they only need to become the place where consumers decide what to buy.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Threat to Amazon is margin (ads/discovery), not fulfillment share; watch retail ad revenue rather than unit volume.
insights.quote: AI assistants don’t need to replicate Amazon’s warehouses to put pressure on Amazon’s profits. They need to become the place where you decide what to buy.
insights.locator: When the power dynamics shift around

insights.claim: Agents such as Muse, ChatGPT, Grok Bot and Instinct cannot rebuild fulfillment networks, but they can compare existing providers and route orders among those that meet a customer's needs.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Agents act as routing layers atop incumbents' infrastructure, commoditizing the front end.
insights.quote: They can compare existing providers and route orders among those that meet the customer’s needs.
insights.locator: Muse, ChatGPT, Grok Bot and Instinct

insights.claim: In an agentic future, an assistant could pick a restaurant, place the order via Toast, pay via Toast and arrange delivery via DoorDash Drive, so the consumer never browses a marketplace or sees a sponsored listing.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Sponsored-listing ad revenue at marketplaces is at risk even when the marketplace still fulfills.
insights.quote: You never browse a marketplace or see a sponsored listing.
insights.locator: The future state isn’t hard to imagine

insights.claim: Incumbents like Amazon, DoorDash and Instacart may keep their fulfillment advantage, but that does not guarantee they preserve their profit pool.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Operational moats may not protect earnings; valuation multiples tied to ad margins could compress.
insights.quote: The incumbents may maintain their fulfillment advantage, but that does not guarantee preserving their profit pool.
insights.locator: The incumbents may maintain their fulfillment

insights.claim: The authors expect the underlying commerce networks to remain valuable but are less sure those networks keep the same share of the economics once someone else brings the customer.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Expect value share to shift from marketplaces toward agent/aggregation layers over time.
insights.quote: I expect the underlying networks to remain valuable. I’m less sure they keep the same share of the economics once someone else brings the customer.
insights.locator: I expect the underlying networks

themes.theme: Advertising is the profit pool at stake

insights.claim: In 2025 Amazon generated $69 billion in advertising revenue versus $34 billion in operating income excluding AWS; at an assumed 70% contribution margin, advertising contributed more than reported operating income.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Amazon's non-AWS profit is essentially an ad business; agent-driven loss of discovery hits earnings disproportionately.
insights.quote: In 2025, Amazon generated $69 billion in advertising revenue compared to $34 billion in operating income ex-AWS.
insights.locator: The incumbents may maintain their fulfillment

insights.claim: The same dynamic, where advertising contributes more than reported operating income, is true for DoorDash and Instacart.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: DoorDash and Instacart profitability is highly sensitive to loss of in-app ad impressions.
insights.quote: The same is true for DoorDash and Instacart.
insights.locator: The incumbents may maintain their fulfillment

insights.claim: Alphabet and Meta combined for nearly $500 billion in advertising revenue in 2025 from being the center of gravity for distribution, and even a meaningful partial redistribution of such flows could fund an entirely new business model and competitive ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: A shift of even a slice of the ~$500B ad pool to agents is a venture-scale opportunity and a risk to Alphabet/Meta.
insights.quote: In 2025, Alphabet and Meta combined for nearly $500 billion in advertising revenue from being the center of gravity for distribution.
insights.locator: Advertising revenue and commissions are key

insights.claim: Whether a platform welcomes AI agents depends on two dimensions: how much incremental demand the agent can bring, and how much of the platform's operating income comes from commissions and advertising tied to controlling discovery and screen time.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Screen for exposure: high ad/commission share of operating income plus low incremental demand = most at risk.
insights.quote: what percentage of your operating income is commissions and/or ad revenue?
insights.locator: Whether you like this or not

insights.claim: Even when a marketplace still handles fulfillment, routing customers around its storefront (e.g., via Toast plus DoorDash Drive) pressures its commissions and advertising; a16z's Seema has called the enterprise-software analogue 'going headless'.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Headless commerce shifts revenue from high-margin marketplace take to lower-margin logistics.
insights.quote: That puts pressure on commissions and advertising even if DoorDash still handles the order.
insights.locator: That changes the options available to agents

themes.theme: Who leans in vs. who blocks

insights.claim: Amazon banned the Muse assistant while Shopify, which lacks a scaled ad business at risk, welcomed the integration.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Corporate stances toward agents reveal where each firm's profit pool sits.
insights.quote: Everyone saw the contrast last week, when Amazon said, “Muse is banned!” while Shopify
insights.locator: When the power dynamics shift around

insights.claim: Instacart is integrating with Muse while Amazon is blocking it, and both choices can make economic sense: Amazon has breadth and habit-driven negotiating leverage, while Instacart has more room to gain orders that don't already start on its marketplace.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Smaller-share marketplaces are natural agent partners; dominant ones negotiate from strength.
insights.quote: The early split is telling: Instacart is integrating with Muse, while Amazon is attempting to block it. Both choices can make economic sense.
insights.locator: The early split is telling

insights.claim: If Amazon ever welcomes Muse back, it will probably preserve some of the old economics because an assistant that cannot buy from Amazon is less useful to customers.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Amazon likely to extract favorable terms from agents rather than lose its take entirely.
insights.quote: if it ever welcomes Muse back, it’ll probably preserve some of the old economics
insights.locator: The early split is telling

insights.claim: Commerce software providers like Shopify, Toast and Square benefit from agents because they open another sales channel while continuing to earn software and payments revenue, with no marketplace advertising business to protect.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Merchant-infrastructure players are structural winners of agentic commerce.
insights.quote: There is no comparable marketplace advertising business to protect.
insights.locator: Shopify, Toast and Square have

insights.claim: Domino's long held out from DoorDash and Uber Eats to protect its customer relationship, but eventually joined for discovery and acquisition while keeping its loyalty program on its own platforms; agents could now put DoorDash on the other side of that same negotiation.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: History suggests holdouts eventually join new demand channels on negotiated terms.
insights.quote: Agents could now put DoorDash on the other side of the same negotiation.
insights.locator: Domino’s was arguably the most important

insights.claim: Incentives differ from bargaining power: a platform may want an assistant's demand, but terms depend on whether the assistant has credible alternative fulfillment options.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Agents with multiple fulfillment options get better terms; sole-source inventory holders keep leverage.
insights.quote: A company can welcome another sales channel while negotiating hard to preserve its economics.
insights.locator: Those incentives are different from bargaining power

themes.theme: Agent economics: new demand vs. rerouted orders

insights.claim: An agent that brings a marketplace a new customer is attractive even on worse terms, whereas one that intercepts an order the marketplace would have won anyway leaves it delivering the same order for less profit.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Key metric to watch: incrementality of agent-sourced orders.
insights.quote: For a marketplace, an agent can bring a new customer (great) or intercept an order it would have won anyway (less so).
insights.locator: Who welcomes another channel

insights.claim: Instacart has seen orders placed with its AI assistant include more items and exceed the value of its typical basket.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Early evidence agentic ordering may lift basket size, partly offsetting lost ad margin.
insights.quote: Instacart has seen orders placed with its AI assistant include more items than Instacart’s typical basket and exceed its typical basket value.
insights.locator: We know that customers will sometimes pay

insights.claim: A fee paid by consumers to an assistant would not replace a marketplace's lost advertising profit; some spend would need to flow to the marketplace or be offset by more volume or cost savings.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Agent monetization and marketplace monetization compete for the same consumer wallet.
insights.quote: But that fee to the assistant would not replace the marketplace’s lost advertising profit.
insights.locator: We know that customers will sometimes pay

insights.claim: Less human browsing could mean more buying, because assistants remove remaining friction like researching, comparing, coordinating and checking out, turning stalled intent into transactions.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Upside case: agents expand total commerce volume, enlarging the pie for all parties.
insights.quote: There is an optimistic possibility: less human browsing could mean more buying.
insights.locator: There is an optimistic possibility

insights.claim: A marketplace might earn less per order but more in total if assistants generate enough additional purchases to offset profit lost on business that would have happened anyway.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Model marketplaces on total profit dollars, not per-order take rate, under agent scenarios.
insights.quote: A marketplace might earn less on each order but more in total if assistants generate enough additional purchases.
insights.locator: That could change the economics

insights.claim: Businesses may be acquiring orders rather than customers from agentic traffic: if a user returns to the assistant for the next purchase, the provider must win the order again, so more bookings do not necessarily mean more direct repeat customers.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Agent channels may raise recurring acquisition costs and erode retention-driven LTV.
insights.quote: More bookings would not necessarily mean more customers who return directly.
insights.locator: Moreover, how these economics will shake out

insights.claim: Assistants may also charge providers for access to their customers, with outcomes depending on how much business each side needs from the other.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Agents could become a new paid-acquisition channel, akin to search ads.
insights.quote: Assistants may also charge providers for access to their customers.
insights.locator: An assistant cannot assume fulfillment remains

insights.claim: If Expedia pays an assistant instead of Google for a booking it merely swaps acquisition costs, but if an assistant charges for an Airbnb booking that would have arrived directly, it adds a new cost.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: OTAs reliant on paid search may be neutral; direct-traffic brands like Airbnb face net new costs.
insights.quote: If Expedia pays an assistant instead of Google to acquire a booking, it may be replacing one acquisition cost with another.
insights.locator: Travel illustrates how these forces

insights.claim: Airbnb's differentiated inventory may give it both strong negotiating leverage over assistants and a strong incentive to protect its direct customer relationships.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Unique inventory is the best defense against agent disintermediation.
insights.quote: Airbnb could therefore have both a strong negotiating position and a strong incentive to protect its direct customer relationships.
insights.locator: Travel illustrates how these forces

insights.claim: Existing physical infrastructure is double-edged: it gives bargaining leverage but requires volume to stay utilized, so Amazon would rather keep an order without ad margin than lose it and spread fixed costs over fewer orders.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: High fixed-cost operators may ultimately concede economics to agents to protect utilization.
insights.quote: This is a double-edged sword for bargaining power
insights.locator: A third consideration is physical infrastructure

insights.claim: Assistants cannot assume fulfillment will remain available on today's terms; gaps may be absorbed through higher fees, lower profits or reduced investment.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Agent unit economics face supplier-repricing risk.
insights.quote: An assistant cannot assume fulfillment remains available tomorrow on the same terms it can get today.
insights.locator: An assistant cannot assume fulfillment remains

insights.claim: The profit pools incumbents are defending could support an entirely new generation of commerce companies built on the infrastructure those incumbents made possible.
insights.speaker: Alex Immerman, Santiago Rodriguez
insights.so_what: Venture opportunity in agentic commerce startups capturing redistributed ad/commission dollars.
insights.quote: the profit pools incumbents are defending could also support an entirely new generation of commerce companies
